title: Zazen
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the basic practice of zazen, opening with Pablo Neruda's poem "Keeping Quiet" and the Buddha sitting under the Bodhi tree. Kanho follows Bodhidharma's exchange with Emperor Wu, who asks what merit he has gained and hears "No merit," before Bodhidharma sits facing a wall for nine years. Practical instruction on posture comes next: the tripod of stability, the straight spine, the tucked chin, and the cosmic mudra, which Abbot Steve at Green Gulch once called out. Kanho then turns to thoughts, which are never stopped, and to counting the breath like loosely holding a puppy's leash. Two more Neruda poems close the evening, the last asking how long the rhinoceros lasts after being moved to compassion.

sentences.text: I really want to thank Tim for switching from our theme of the year, which is ancestors, with an emphasis on women ancestors, to talks about basic practice, basic zazen, Fukanzazengi.
I really appreciate it, because there are so many new faces here, which is super great.
I'm really enjoying that.
So all of you who are new, a big warm welcome to you all.
And if you're not so new, a big warm welcome to you too.
It's so great to see all these old and new faces here.

Since I wanted to stay in this theme of basic practice, I was writing a talk, and I was writing, and it's not long enough, it's not long enough, and I wrote more, and I wrote more, and now I'm sorry to inform you: it's too long.
So I'll probably nip off the last part.
Maybe someone could give me a heads-up when we're five minutes ahead of time.
I have to watch, but I don't want to look at it.
Those of you who have been hanging out with me know that I like my poems to be part of Dharma talks.
I should correct this: these are not my poems.
I wouldn't want you to suffer that badly.
So tonight it's Pablo Neruda, and since we're talking about zazen, the first poem I chose is "Keeping Quiet."
*Now we will count to 12, and we will all keep still.
For once on the face of the earth, let's not speak in any language.
Let's stop for a second and not move our arms so much.
It would be an exotic moment without rush, without engines.*
*We would all be together in a sudden strangeness.
Fishermen in the cold sea would not harm whales, and a man gathering salt would look at his hurt hands.
Those who prepare green wars, wars with gas, wars with fire, victories with no survivors, would put on clean clothes and walk about with their brothers in the shade doing nothing.*
*What I want should not be confused with total inactivity.
Life is what it is about.
I want no truck with death.

If we were not so single-minded about keeping our lives moving and for once could do nothing, perhaps a huge silence might interrupt the sadness of never understanding ourselves and of threatening ourselves with death.*
*Perhaps the earth can teach us as when everything seems dead and later proves to be alive.
Now I'll count up to 12, and you keep quiet, and I will go.*
So we all experience some zazen tonight, and we've been exploring it together.
Zazen is not separate from our life.
It is the activity of life itself when we stop running away from it.
Zazen is not a technique to calm the mind or to escape the world.
It is the world sitting as you.
It is life clarifying itself through your sitting body and breathing heart.
Yeah, I know it's the lungs, but the heart sounds a lot better.
So let us begin under the Bodhi tree.
Siddhartha Gautama had exhausted every austerity and every spiritual practice.
Finally, he simply sat down.
He bowed.
"Even if my blood and flesh dry up, I will not rise from this seat until I realize the way."
That moment when the Buddha sat down and did not run away is the archetype of zazen.
He did not sit because it was comfortable.
He sat because he had stopped fleeing his own life.
And each time we sit down, we re-enact that same bow.
We stop running.
Zazen is a training ground where we learn to meet discomfort without retreat.
So when your knee is hurt and you really don't want to sit, especially when you're at home and nobody is watching, and you want to rearrange your sock drawer, we don't.
We learn to live with those little discomforts, so that when the true pain that we cannot escape comes up, we have practiced how to bear it.
We sit down with fear, boredom, pain, and we learn to allow them to unfold inside awareness.
So for those of you who have not been around so long, this is not a contest on how much pain you can endure.
If you have the feeling that whatever you're doing is damaging your body, please make an intentional move to rearrange yourself to continue sitting.
One of the zazen sayings is, "When you sit, sit.
When you stand, stand.
Above all, don't wobble."
So if you really cannot sit anymore, don't do those little micro-wiggles.
They don't help for more than ten seconds.
Do a little bow.
Rearrange your legs into a different position.
In fact, pulling up one knee like this is really great to take a break in the middle of your sitting, and it's perfectly fine to do that.
Try not to annoy your neighbors, but if you do, it's good for their practice.
My teacher, Norman Fischer, said this line that really imprinted itself on me.
He said, "Practice means to turn toward that which is difficult."
Our instinct, if something is uncomfortable, if we don't like something, is to avoid it at all costs.
When we see that unpleasant thing coming up, we just turn around and boogie.
That's not the Zen way.
The Zen way is to fully turn towards it, to get to know it, to become intimate with it.
So that's what we practice on our cushion.
When we turn toward what we would rather avoid, we discover that we can rest in something larger than comfort or discomfort.
We find that peace does not come from control, but from being intimate.

And wouldn't you know, even if you're in the most comfortable position imaginable, if you're sitting on the sofa or lying in bed, having a meal with friends, at some point it will become uncomfortable.
You will want to get up and do something different.
So escaping into comfort simply does not work.
The Buddha's sitting was not heroic endurance, but gentle staying with whatever arose.
His enlightenment beneath the morning star was not an addition to his sitting.
It was the sitting itself.
Reality shone through because he did not try to move away from it.
Centuries later, in China, Bodhidharma carried the same vow.
When he met Emperor Wu of Liang, the emperor proudly asked, "Since my accession to the throne, I have built many temples, copied countless sutras, and supported innumerable monks.
What merit have I gained?"
Bodhidharma replied, "No merit."
The emperor was startled and asked, "Why no merit?"
And Bodhidharma told him that these are just small accomplishments with limited rewards, their shadows following form.
Not real.
You can imagine the emperor, he was probably pretty upset.
And he wanted to challenge Bodhidharma, probably.
So he asked him, "What is the highest meaning of the holy truth?"
Bodhidharma said, "Vast emptiness, nothing holy."
The emperor said, "Who is this who is standing before me?"
Bodhidharma replied, "I don't know."
He then left the palace, crossed the Yangtze River, and sat facing a wall for nine years.
What does it mean to face a wall for nine years?
It is not a withdrawal from life, but complete engagement with it.
That wall is not made from stone.
It is the wall of our resistance, our projections, our wish for things to be different from the way they are.
So obviously, this is a very physical practice.
When I trained to become a mindfulness teacher, I picked up this great line: "We don't have a body, we are a body."
And so how we hold this body in meditation really influences what happens in our mind, believe it or not.
We often talk about zazen as if it were all awareness and lofty aspirations, about the mind being subtle, calm, and clear.
But in Zen, body and mind are not separate.
They are one continuous activity.
When the body settles, the mind settles.
When the body straightens, the mind becomes upright.
When we relax into our sitting, the heart opens.
So when we take our seat, we don't just arrange our body so our mind can meditate.
The body itself is the gate of practice.
We take the seat like the Buddha did under the Bodhi tree.

Whether we sit on a cushion or a chair, our body should have this tripod of stability through our knees and our behind, or our feet and our legs, depending on whether we sit on a bench, a zafu, a chair.
It does not really matter.
Please believe it when it says in the sutras, "Standing or walking, sitting or lying down, there is no difference."
If you can sit on a paper towel, if you're that flexible, that doesn't mean your meditation is better than the person on the chair.
So please, if your body says, "I really want a chair," believe it and work with it.
Every detail of our posture has been handed down through the centuries.
Dogen wrote Fukanzazengi, which Tim has discussed so beautifully, and it gives us very precise instructions.
But that posture is not dogma.
It is a way to express our practice with our whole body.
The Buddha's posture still teaches us today.
So our sitting begins with the base, cushion or chair, does not matter.
Two knees or two feet and the base of our spine.
This tripod grounds us.
The reason why people sit in full lotus is because it's the most stable of positions possible, followed by half lotus, Burmese, Seiza, it all works.
In Zen, we say our spine should be straight.
When we say straight, we don't mean straight as an arrow, but straight following the natural curve of our spine.
Our head is on top of the spine, obviously.
Imagine that with the top of your head, you are pushing up a cloud.
Is there anything you can do so it doesn't scratch all the time?
So we imagine that we're pushing up a cloud with the top of our head.
Or sometimes people say that you have like a thread attached to the top of your head, and it's just keeping us straight.
When we talk about keeping the head on top of our spine, we don't want the crown of our head to be the top, but just up here.
Sorry, I'm not very eloquent at times.
Also, it's tempting, especially with our zafu, if our cushion is not high enough, to slouch like this.
Well, let's try this.
Thank you very much for the adjustment.
So, where was I?
Ah, yeah, the head.
Oh, and one really interesting thing.
We lift our spine and make ourselves a little taller in our seat and bring our shoulders back a little.
We really open up our chest so we can breathe more smoothly.
Believe it or not, for years I struggled with having a smooth breath.
It always got stuck by the throat.
And all of a sudden there was all this space and this smooth in and out flow of breath.
It takes practice, it takes time, it takes adjustments.
So, energy flows, breath flows, mind clears.
This is the physical expression of our practice.
Collectedness, it arises out of balance.
It's not something we push for.
It's a natural alignment of body and mind.
Thank you.
This is really perfect now.
Now, quite louder?
All right.
So, one thing you might find interesting is also when you sit and your chin drifts up.
If I see someone sitting like this, I want to walk up and say, "Whoo-hoo, you're daydreaming."
It is really bizarre how that works.
As soon as the chin comes up, your mind goes to the jungle, it goes to China, it goes on world tour.
So, keep the chin just slightly tucked in, your gaze slightly downward.
Don't fixate your view on any material object.
It can be in midair.
This gentle downward gaze, not staring, not wandering.
That's what we're shooting for.
The Buddha is often shown like that in statues.
In the same way, our posture expresses a quiet attentiveness to our body, to our breath, to our mind, as if saying, "I'm here.
I'm listening."
So, you maybe wonder why we hold our hands like this.
This is called the cosmic mudra, left hand on top of the right, thumb tips slightly touching.
Imagine you're holding like a little Post-it or something between your thumbs.
Just the lightest touch.
But if you don't pay attention, you'll find your thumbs drifting apart, your chin coming up, and off you go.
So, one must pay attention to it, otherwise it misbehaves.
The other way your hands might misbehave, you look down and you see your thumb tips are wide from pressing together so hard, and your whole body is knotted up.
I remember Abbot Steve at Green Gulch.
He used to sometimes pass through the meditation hall, and then all of a sudden you would hear from somewhere, "Look at your mudra!"
So pay attention to the mudra.
And then our breath.
Have I mentioned the breath yet?
It's not something we control.
If you believe that you're controlling your breath, just try to stop breathing for five minutes or so, so you do not control it.
And it's not a performance.
You don't try to impress anybody with your breathing, but it can really support your practice.
Don't do any special breathing for Zen.
Just a natural, smooth in and out press.
You might notice that it becomes naturally slower, and that's great.
But don't try to breathe slowly.
It's not the destination.
It's also not about forcing the mind to be still.
It is about allowing the body to express stillness so the mind can follow.
Dogen said, "When you practice the way in body and mind, the whole world becomes practice."
So each part of our posture is a doorway.
The solid seat says, "I belong to this earth."
The straight spine says, "Wake up."
And the tucked chin says, "I'm willing to be right here for as long as it takes."
When body and mind come together like this, it is continuous activity.
When the body settles, the mind settles.
When we take our seat, we're not just arranging our body.
The body is the gate of practice.
It has been said that our zazen is the reenactment ritual of the Buddha's awakening.
So when you sit down, you are the Buddha on your seat.
Trust your body.
Trust your breath.
Let zazen sit you.
Zazen may look like stillness, but it's actually the movement of compassion itself.
When we sit upright and still, we are not withdrawing from the world.
We are leaning into it with our whole body, without movement.
The stillness of zazen is alive.
It breathes.
It listens.
It includes everything.
Dogen says in the fascicle Bendowa, "When even one person sits upright in samadhi, the mind of the whole world is turned upright."
That's how powerful this simple act can be.
Just one person sitting, breathing quietly, can tilt the whole world a little bit closer to sanity.
When we stop running from what's uncomfortable, when we stay with what's here instead of trying to fix it or flee from it, something in the fabric of the world steadies too.
And the world can feel that.
To sit is an embodiment of compassion.
Not the kind that tries to rescue a puppy for the camera on the YouTube channel, but the kind that holds everything exactly as it is, reality itself.
Each time we sit still, we are saying to all beings, silently, without words, "This too belongs."
The ache in my knees belongs.
My wandering thoughts, my world travel on the cushion into the jungle, belong.
The sorrow of the world belongs.
Our tears belong.
And in that quiet belonging, compassion moves.
Light, wordless, and awake.
When we sit zazen, something very quiet begins to happen inside.
At first, and it might take years, it doesn't seem like much, and most of the time we don't even notice it.
The thoughts are still there.
The body still aches.
The world is still noisy.
But underneath all that movement, the mind begins to soften and the heart begins to open.
We take down our walls inside.
We create space.
Not space as in detachment, but space as in spaciousness.
Room for life to breathe.
Room for others to exist, just the way they are.
It's not our job to fix other people or to judge them.
We have room for the heart to feel what it has been holding back.
When we allow everything to be exactly as it is, the mind stops tightening around its own old habits.
The space between thoughts opens.
And within that space, we can find a tenderness we did not create.
It's always been there.
This is how zazen made me more human.
It didn't give me a new personality or a new set of beliefs.
It gave me more space to be real.
Grief can move throughout our heart without freezing it.
Joy can appear without us clinging to it.
Because there is space, we can listen.
We can pause before responding.
We can meet another person, their fear, their pain, their joy, without trying to fix them or change them.
So zazen doesn't make us superhuman.
All those sages of old, they're wonderful.
I love all their old Zen stories.
But it was their Zen stories.
We've got to make our own.
With the body we have, with the mind we have, and with the world as it is right now.
The more we sit, the more we can learn how to stay open in the middle of difficulty.
And that's how the world changes.
Not by force, but by presence.
So please, each time you take the seat, remember, you're helping to make a little bit more room in the world.
You're creating space for all beings to be held in kindness just the way they are.
Or am I doing time-lapse?
Yay?
Okay.
Oh my God.
So now we've talked about the body quite a bit.
So what do we do with our mind?
We talked a little bit about that too.
We talked about what we do with our hands, how to breathe.
What about the mind?
What am I supposed to do with all these thoughts that pop up nonstop?
And people often say, "I could never ever meditate.
I could not stop my mind from thinking."
Well, maybe I'm spilling the beans, but you really don't stop your mind.
Just like your saliva glands produce saliva, your brain will produce thoughts.
And it's really easy for us to be stoic and sit here and let like 95% of thoughts just float by one after the other.
But then comes that hook with a very special bait, and we go for it.
We just go for it.
And we pursue that poor little thought until it gives up, rolls over and dies.
So what do we do with all those thoughts?
We don't reject them and we don't pursue them.
So how do we usually think?
Like I might think, "I need to pick up the jacket from the dry cleaner."
If I'm in zazen, the thought should end there.
I don't repeat it.
I just let the thought come up and it disappears.
At home, I go, "I should pick up the jacket.
I wonder if they got that spot out.
I remember when so-and-so spilled that soup on me and I tried to get it out of the jacket.
Damn, they're so clumsy.
Why did they do that?
And now I have to pay for the jacket to get cleaned and I have to drive into town and I don't feel like it and it's raining outside."
That's how we usually think.
Does this sound familiar to anybody here?
I guess so.
So the mind will think, but don't chase the thought, and watch out for that special bait.
It's hard to resist.
But here's the great news.
You will absolutely 100% get lost chasing your thoughts.
It's what happens.
It's what happens.
But here's the beautiful thing.
At some point, you will remember, "Oh, I'm doing zazen.
I'm not supposed to chase my thoughts."
And that is the beautiful part.
That's the moment of mindfulness that fully puts you back onto the cushion, into this moment, and not to the dry cleaners or the restaurant or whatever else happens.
And we are never harsh to ourselves when we have lost our [unclear: "mental weight"].
We don't say, "Oh, I'm so bad at this.
Look at all these other people.
They are so good, but I'm really, really bad."
We don't do that because one, it's unkind, and two, [unclear: "you don't read thoughts"].
Just be kind.
Treat your mind like you would treat a little puppy or like you would treat a two-year-old.
When they misbehave, you don't go, "Whack, behave."
No, you're very gentle.
You bring them back and you say, "Stay here, right here, come back."
And then you carry on.
Don't beat yourself up over getting lost in your mind, getting lost in thoughts, because it will happen and it's perfectly all right that it does.
Every time we realize that the mind has drifted and we bring it back, that is a moment of mindfulness, of being right here.
If you need some more help to occupy your mind, you might want to count your breath.
Count every exhale from one to ten.
The great reward if you reach ten is you get to go back to one.
Also, if you find that you are at twenty-seven, go back to one.
If you realize you've been menu planning, doing HR in your mind, getting into politics, whatever it is, just come back and be right here.
The goal is not to get to ten.
I can tell you there have been periods of zazen I didn't get past three.
I've been at this for twenty-five years.
Counting my breath is still how I start pretty much every period of zazen.
And it's pretty miraculous.
When I'm out in the big wide world and the fecal matter is hitting the air distribution system, if I go to counting my breath, my whole body goes, "Oh, I know what I'm supposed to do now."
And it just gives me a little bit of a safety net.
It's like holding my hand.
It's just helping me to stabilize in the middle of chaos.
So I was thinking of this, and I'm rather proud of this: counting my breath is like loosely holding that puppy's leash, so it doesn't stray too far.
Not too tight, not too slack.
Another way to practice, since some people really don't like practicing with breath, is sound meditation.
Instead of watching your breath, you watch everything you hear.
The hiss of the AC, the car driving by, bird chirping, the heater coming on, whatever it is.
Every sound is okay.
There is not a single sound that is not acceptable.
The phone rings, the phone rings.
And we just stay with the sound the same way we would stay with breath.
One minute?
That means I'm going to skip Dogen.
So I'm going to skip Dogen.
But I think you should hear another poem.
I'm still with Pablo Neruda.
*Through a closed mouth the flies enter.*
*Why, with those red flames at hand, are rubies so hard to burn?
Why does the heart of the topaz reveal a yellow honeycomb?
Why does the rose amuse itself, changing the color of its streams?
Why does the emerald shiver like a drowned submarine?*
*Why does the sky grow pale under the June stars?
Where does a lizard's tail get its fresh supply of paint?
Where is the underground fire that revives the carnations?
Where does the salt acquire the transparency of its glands?*
*Where did the cold sleep that it awoke so dark?
And where, where, its stripes of mourning, its stripes of gold.*
And there's one more little poem, and that's out of Pablo Neruda's book of questions.
It's like my favorite two lines of his.
And I think it makes a great poem, too.
*How long does the rhinoceros last after he's moved to compassion?*
So if you heard something tonight that supports your practice and might help you in your practice, please enjoy it.
And if you've known all this or it didn't land, please forget every word I said and just return to your practice with a joyous heart.
